clue.text: Scallywag lost in search for a scallywag

indicators.note: something lost in a crowd is swallowed up by it, so the wanted word lies buried inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of 'for' and into 'a' and 'scallywag'

explanation.surface: Someone combing the streets for a missing rogue, only for the rogue to vanish again.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in foR A SCALlywag; the repeated 'scallywag' is both definition and part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: A rascal and a scallywag are both playful words for a mischievous rogue or scamp.

clue.text: This bomb is part of Nato munitions

definitions.note: the answer is the word that goes before 'bomb'

indicators.note: the wanted word forms a part of the run of letters that follows

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of Nato and the start of munitions

explanation.surface: A military briefing on which weapon is held in the alliance's stockpile.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden in nATO Munitions. 'This bomb' points to the kind of bomb named by the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An atom bomb is the nuclear fission weapon, so this word names that particular kind of bomb.

clue.text: Decomposed coat found in Cambridgeshire burial vaults

indicators.note: something decomposed has broken down, so the letters of the word are broken up and rearranged
one thing found in another sits inside it, so the reshuffled word goes inside the county abbreviation

blocks.note: the letters of coat rearranged
the standard abbreviation of the county name

explanation.surface: A rotting coat discovered in an East Anglian tomb.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambridgeshire is an English county with a standard short form; the jumbled coat is placed after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Catacombs are underground cemeteries made of tunnels and chambers where the dead were laid to rest.

blocks.note: L stands for learner, as on a British learner driver's plate
to merit something is to earn it

explanation.surface: A schoolchild being awarded good marks for their work.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, a learner driver displays an L plate, so L can stand for any pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: To study a subject is to learn it, both verbs in the third person singular here.

clue.text: He can make rifles and thin mugs

indicators.note: to make something out of materials is to form them into a new shape, so the letters that follow are formed anew

blocks.note: all eight letters used

explanation.surface: A versatile craftsman who turns out both firearms and delicate drinking vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make' does double duty: it belongs to the definition and also signals the rearrangement of thin mugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunsmith is a craftsman who builds and repairs firearms such as rifles.

blocks.note: golden can mean excellent, as in a golden opportunity
a direct synonym

explanation.surface: High praise for a lovely piece of fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Golden Delicious is a well-known variety of yellow eating apple sold worldwide.

blocks.note: a chip or small notch in an edge is a nick
the usual abbreviation on forms
the 'to' is dropped; me taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone protesting that the nickname Chip doesn't suit them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chip' in quotes looks like the nickname itself, but it is a synonym for a small cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A soubriquet (or sobriquet) is an informal name given to someone in place of their real one.

clue.text: French revolutionary leader married a traitor

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for married
taken as written
a rat is someone who betrays their side

explanation.surface: A scandalous revelation that a revolutionary figure wed a turncoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Paul Marat was a radical journalist and politician of the French Revolution, murdered in his bath.

clue.text: Involve me, an idiot at heart, in Tory shenanigans

indicators.note: the short word involves, or wraps around, the word for an idiot placed at its heart
at the heart of one word and then in another means each piece goes into the middle of the next

blocks.note: taken as written
a fool is an idiot
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone protesting about being dragged into Conservative party antics.
explanation.walkthrough: Two nested insertions: the idiot goes inside 'me', and the result goes into the middle of the party name. A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomfoolery and shenanigans both mean silly or mischievous behaviour, the kind of foolish carry-on that is not serious.

blocks.note: the foot of something is its end, as the foot of a bed
a ball is a formal dancing party

explanation.surface: Someone giving up dance lessons in favour of games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End to dancing' reads as stopping dancing, but End and dancing are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Football is a team game, whether soccer, rugby or the American kind, so it is one example of a sport.

indicators.note: unorthodox means not in the usual form, so the letters of the word before it are put in an unusual order

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for church
the letters of more rearranged

explanation.surface: A church that has rather more unconventional ingredients in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church' and 'unorthodox' suggest religion, but neither is about faith here.
explanation.definitionFit: Chrome is the everyday name for chromium, the metallic chemical element, and also its plating.

indicators.note: dissolute means loose-living, so the following names are loosened and their letters set free to rearrange

blocks.note: every letter of the three words used

explanation.surface: A disapproving verdict on a pair of debauched friends.
explanation.definitionFit: Censure and condemnation are both nouns for strong, formal expression of disapproval.

indicators.note: distressed means upset or knocked about, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: all ten letters used

explanation.surface: An upset woman who needs to settle down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'calm' is the noun here, the state of being calm.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedateness is a noun for composure and quiet steadiness, matching calm used as a noun.

blocks.note: first meaning: a word used for something
second meaning: a period of the academic year

explanation.walkthrough: Hilary looks like a person's name, but Hilary is the spring term at Oxford and some other British universities and law courts.
explanation.definitionFit: A term is a word naming a thing, and also a division of the academic year such as Hilary or Michaelmas.

clue.text: Stupid boy initially taking ell to be a weight

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

blocks.note: a direct synonym
the first letter only
taken as written; an ell is an old unit of length

explanation.surface: A dim lad mistaking an old measure for a unit of mass.
explanation.walkthrough: An ell is a length, not a weight, which makes the surface absurd.
explanation.definitionFit: A dumbbell is a short bar with weights at each end, lifted in exercise, so it is a weight.

clue.text: Boffin with tendency to produce bright idea

blocks.note: a brain is a very clever person; boffin is British slang for a scientist or expert
a wave is a trend or general movement, as in a wave of opinion

explanation.surface: A scientist whose inclinations lead to inspired thinking.
explanation.definitionFit: A brainwave is a sudden clever thought or inspiration, the same as a bright idea.

blocks.note: taken as written
the standard abbreviation for female
fluent movement is smooth and graceful

explanation.surface: A description of an elegant, wealthy woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Affluent means wealthy or well off, a direct synonym of rich as an adjective.

clue.text: Frail sap transformed into opera hero

indicators.note: something transformed takes on a new form, so the letters given are recast in a new order

blocks.note: all eight letters used

explanation.surface: A weakling who turns into the leading man of an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, Wagner's hero begins as a naive 'pure fool'.
explanation.definitionFit: Parsifal is the title character of Wagner's last opera, the innocent knight who wins the Grail.

clue.text: Ethereal Titania, perhaps without a head

indicators.note: lacking a head means the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: Titania is queen of the fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream, so she is an example

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's fairy queen pictured as a delicate, otherworldly figure, perhaps decapitated.
explanation.walkthrough: FAIRY loses its first letter F.
explanation.definitionFit: Airy and ethereal both describe something light, delicate and insubstantial, as if made of air.

blocks.note: to wilt is to droop and lose vigour
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone lounging listlessly on a rug.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilton is a town in Wiltshire, England, famous for its woven carpets.
explanation.definitionFit: A Wilton is a type of woven pile carpet named after the town where it was first made.

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
an assembly of things is a collection

explanation.surface: A memory of a school assembly or a parliamentary gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital A on Assembly suggests a parliament; it simply means a gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: A recollection is a memory, the thing a person calls back to mind.

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O
to pine is to waste away from longing

explanation.surface: A lover confesses their feelings and is then left to languish.
explanation.definitionFit: To opine is to state an opinion, a formal way to declare what one thinks.

blocks.note: first meaning: to say or relate
second meaning: the legendary Swiss crossbowman

explanation.surface: A question of which country claims a national hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a noun for a country, but it is the verb meaning say.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell is to state or say; William Tell is the legendary Swiss marksman who shot an apple from his son's head.

clue.text: Field redeveloped up to a point in the valley

definitions.note: strictly a narrow pass through a valley or gorge

indicators.note: redeveloped land is rebuilt in a new layout, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
E for east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A field in a valley being built on, but only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up to a point' reads as 'partly'; it splits into a joining 'up to' and 'a point', a compass direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A defile is a narrow gorge or pass through hills, a steep-sided cut in a valley.

clue.text: Deeply offended openly gay newspaper editor

blocks.note: someone who is out is open about being gay
a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper
the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A gay newspaper editor angered by something, perhaps a hostile story.
explanation.definitionFit: Outraged means extremely angry or affronted, the strongest form of being deeply offended.

clue.text: Arsenic tops osmium as a cause of lung cancer

blocks.note: As is the chemical symbol for arsenic
to top is to best or beat
Os is the chemical symbol for osmium

explanation.surface: A ranking of toxic elements by how much harm they do to the lungs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tops' looks like a noun but is the verb, to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestos is a fibrous mineral once used in insulation whose inhaled fibres are known to cause lung cancer.

definitions.note: the answer is the verb meaning to annoy

blocks.note: to need to do something is to have to, or must
le is a French word for the

explanation.surface: An exasperated question about whether the French have to be irritating.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle someone is to provoke or irritate them with persistent jibes.
